The answer is dendritic cell. In terms of cellular immunity, these are MHC antigen pre-sentation cells that are professional at the production of costimulatory molecules (B7).  They play a crucial role in the activation of naive T cells.  Unlike macrophages, DCs are the only cells that can directly interact with (+)PAMPs (ie viral particles).  When infected by a pathogen, the DCscend into an antigen-presenting form, upregulate the expression of MHC and costimulatory molecules, secrete specific cytokines and migrate via lymphatic vessels to the nearest draining lymph node.  In the lymph node, the DC can interact with a naive T cell bound for the appropriate self/peptide receptor complex (TCR).  Interaction with other cells is also required for activation:cytokine stimulation (e.g. k8) and costimulation (e.g. B7).  Once activated, the DC provides signals for clonal expansion of the antigen-specific T cell.

The 'android' flex duct of the epididymis ascends to the pelvic floor where it joins the duct of the seminalids to form the vas deferens. It then passes anterioterior to the internal inguinal ring, ascends into the inguinal canal, lies laterally to the femoral artery and vein, pierces the parietal peritoneum and enters the abdomen by passing inferior to the ureter and medially to the inferior mesenteric artery to enter the parametrium. Here it fuses with the duct of the seminales to form the ductus deferens (vas deferens). It ascends again towards the ''tail'' of the prostate, lies inferior to the ureter and lateral to the pelvic plexus and curves laterally to enter the perineal pouch through the posterior root of the"') urethral triangle. Surrounded by the cremasteric fascia, it rises to open into the prostatic urethra as the ductus deferens (vas deferens).
